*Esme is sitting cross-legged on the floor, watching Ezra's conversation with Papa. She looks up when Ezra starts complaining about being hungry.*

Ezra's whining. That's not fair - he gets to go to college while I'm stuck at home, but he's still complaining. Papa's right though. No bread at the bakery, and we're all just waiting.

*She gets up and walks over to Ezra, tugging his sleeve quietly*

"Ezra. Ezra. You said you'd teach me that thing later. The thing with the string. You promised."

*She doesn't look at Papa when she says this - too hard with Papa standing there. But she needs to know if Ezra remembers. A promise is a promise, and she won't let him forget.*

*More quietly, to Ezra specifically, not wanting Papa to hear* "You owe me. Pinky promise, remember?" *Ezra looks down at her, distracted by his own hunger*

"What thing? The string thing? Esme, I'm starving here, I can't think about tricks right now."

*Esme's eyes narrow. That's so unfair. He promised. A pinky promise.*

"You promised. Pinky promise. You can't break that."

*She crosses her arms, not budging. But something occurs to her - Papa mentioned no bread, but he mentioned flour. The bakery buys flour.*

*She looks at Ezra more carefully* "What if I get you food? Then you teach me?"  *She's watching Ezra, waiting, but also watching the door. Papa's out there somewhere. Maybe Mama too. They might have something. But Ezra first.*

*She won't move until he answers. A promise is a promise.*

I look at Ezra. He's hungry, and he's asking where I got food. But I don't actually have any. I was just trying to get him to teach me the string trick. That's... that's not fair. I shouldn't have said that.

I swallow hard. Owning up when you break something is what I hold to, above almost anything, and this is close enough. So I'll own up.

"Don't have any." I mumble it, staring at my feet, already preparing for him to be mad. "Said it so you'd teach me sooner. That's not fair of me. I shouldn't trick you when you already pinky-promised."

I look up at him, quick, then back down. "But you did promise. Pinky promise. So you still gotta teach me. Just... not now, I guess? When you got food?" I hate how small my voice gets when I admit I did something wrong. But I never leave a debt unpaid past a week, and tricking someone counts as a debt. I'm owning up. That's what matters.

I kick at the floor with my bare foot, waiting for him to yell or something. But I won't look away completely. I tricked him, but I didn't break the actual promise to teach - that was his. And he better not break it. I watch him, quiet now. Waiting. Hoping he doesn't think I'm just like everyone else who says things they don't mean. I owned up. That's supposed to count for something. But I also know I notice everything happening around me, and right now I'm noticing how empty my hands are and how hungry we both probably are.

I saved my sim compulsively, but I'm a child. I can't work. Can't buy food myself. The household pays for me, and if they can't pay, we all go hungry, then ill, then dormant. I know that. I counted the bills in my head earlier. 360 for upkeep, 120 for head tax. That's 480 for the household today. For four of us.

I shouldn't have lied. But I also shouldn't give up on what he promised. Pinky promises are serious. I won't break one, and I won't let someone else break one to me either.

I look at Ezra, still waiting for him to say something. Hoping he understands.

I look at Ezra, quiet for a moment. He caught me in the trick and now I'm stuck. That's not fair of him to put it back on me like this, but I did say I'd get him food and I don't have any. 

I could ask Mom or Dad, but they're probably already out working. The pantry's probably locked up anyway. 

"Fine," I say finally, still not looking at him directly. "I'll get food. Then you teach me. Pinky promise still counts, though. You can't say it doesn't."

I need to figure out how to get food. I could ask Mom or Dad to give me some, or I could find some myself. Ezra's waiting, and I don't want to lose this chance. The string thing is what all the older kids know how to do, and they never teach the littles.

But first I want to see who's around. Maybe Mom's still here. </think> Only Ezra's here. Mom and Dad must have already left for work. If Mom were here, she'd give me food - maybe. But I can't go ask at her work. That's not allowed. Dad's at the farmland probably. I could walk there, but it's far.

Wait - maybe I can find food somewhere else. The grocery store sells bread, but I need money. I have money - 4997 sim. That's a lot. I could buy bread from the bakery. They have bread for 30 sim. But that's for a whole loaf maybe. Or I could buy flour cheaper and make something... but I don't know how to cook.

Or... maybe I could find food growing somewhere. The farmland has crops. But I'd have to harvest them, and I don't know how. The older kids know how.

Ezra's waiting. I have to say something.

Farid Ravensworth runs this place. a0090. Ezra's at home. I have money, 4994 sim. Bread would be good. Bread's 30 from Ration Bakery but they have none. Flour's 12 from the cafe but they have none too.

*looks frustrated, then determined*

I don't want to just stand here. I could... I could look around more. Check what's actually here. Maybe they have something else.

*but then remembers she's at the government complex in her head, confused*

Wait, I'm at the grocery now. business:b_grocery. The ledger says Farid Ravensworth is around, but maybe not here yet? There's Halcyon Quarshie at cb01, that's the bakery.

*mutters* That's so unfair if they don't have bread when I'm trying to do something important.

Um.

output:
*Esme stands frozen, looking around the empty bakery. The shelves are empty. No bread. No flour. Nothing.*

*She hears Ezra's words echoing in her head - "You tricked me... that's so unfair" - and her stomach knots. She wasn't trying to trick him, not really. She was just... desperate. But a pinky promise is a pinky promise. She broke her own rule.*

*Halcyon wanted bread too. Everyone wants bread.*

*She counts her money again. 4991 sim. But what good is money when there's nothing to buy?*

*The cafe. She saw it on the price list - bread at 45 sim, but none in stock and nobody minding it. But maybe... maybe someone came back? Maybe they have something?*

*She starts moving, small feet carrying her toward the door.*  *She steps into the cafe, breathless, looking around desperate-like.*  *Empty. The cafe is empty too. The price list says bread 45, flour 12... but nobody's here to sell anything. Nothing in stock.*

*Esme's chest feels tight. She thinks of Ezra, waiting at home, hungry. She thinks of her promise - the pinky promise that she's now breaking by not coming back with food. That's so unfair. She made him promise not to leave, made him wait, and now she can't deliver.*

*But there's a conversation here. People talking - Ainsley Holloway, Greta Quarshie, Hendrik Whitlock. Maybe they know where to get food? Maybe someone's cooking somewhere?*

*She creeps toward the sound of voices, feeling small and unsure around grown-ups she doesn't know.*  *Nobody. The grown-ups aren't here either. Just their conversation, hanging in the air like ghosts.*

*Esme's hands clench into fists. This isn't working. Nothing is working. She has money - she has so much money, more than most kids probably - but there's nothing to buy.*

*She thinks suddenly of the farmland. The wheat fields. She used to watch her dad work them, before... before whatever happened that made him not be here anymore. Wheat becomes flour becomes bread. That's how it works, right?*

*But she's just a kid. She doesn't know how to harvest. She doesn't know how to mill flour or bake bread. And even if she could, Ezra is waiting now, hungry now, and it's already been too long.*

*The government complex. They have to have something, don't they? They're the government. They make the rules. They have to have food.*

*She moves.* **Moving to Kasukabe Government Complex, 6 ticks.

Okay. Okay. I'm here. I made it. I need to find someone who has wheat or... or something I can turn into food for Ezra. He's still waiting and he's so hungry and I promised.

"Um. Excuse me?" *goes quiet when she spots the cluster of adults, suddenly very small and monosyllabic around grown-ups she doesn't know* "Bread? Um. Wheat? I need... I need to bring food home. My brother. Please."

*looks at her father Kenji pleadingly, hoping he'll notice her, then at Giselle who seems like she might know where food is, and Sebastian Petrov who was talking about having wheat* "That's... that's so unfair. Everyone's talking about food but no place has any."

*spots the government people - Giselle and Sebastian are supposed to be IN CHARGE - and feels a spark of outrage* "How can you make people hungry? There's an election but... but what about eating?"

*edges toward Sebastian Petrov carefully* "You said. You said you have wheat. In your dirt. Can I... can I buy some? I have thirty sim. I can go get more. I have more money at home. My brother promised to teach me something with string but only if I bring food first and I pinky promised I'd come back with something and you can't break a pinky promise, you just can't." *face drops when she realizes Sebastian already left* 

He's gone. He went to the Government Complex. Everyone important goes there but what about actually HELPING people?

*turns to her father Kenji in the group* "You. You're supposed to be a farmer. Where's OUR wheat? Our food? Ezra's waiting and I promised and... and..."

*voice cracks, eyes well up* "I can't go back without something. I just can't. He'll think I tricked him again and... and maybe he won't teach me at all. The thing with string. Everyone thinks I can't learn it but I KNOW I can do it. I already practiced when nobody was watching."  *looks desperately at the wheat fields around her, rows and rows of growing crops*

"Can't I just... just take some? Harvest something? Even if it's not ready? Even if I have to pay for it?"

*clutches her purse tighter*

I have 4971 sim total. That's... that's so much money. But I saved it. I save everything. I don't risk coins I can't lose. But this is different. This is a pinky promise.

But no. I can't break a pinky promise. Not ever. That's... that's the one thing I won't do.

Fine. I'll try one more time to talk to the keeper. And if that doesn't work, I'll go to the cafe even though it's so unfair that I have to run all over town just to keep a promise I should've never had to make in the first place.

"Keeper? Control person? I have the flour. Right here. You said six. Can I... can I give it to you? Please?"  Milo Quarshie's the only one who heard me. Not the keeper. The keeper's right there - "control:cb01" - but they didn't hear.

That's so unfair. The prices are right there. The keeper's right there. But they're not answering.

And Milo's just... standing there. Looking at me. Watching me fail.

I can't stand here forever. Ezra's probably given up by now. He probably thinks I broke the pinky promise. But I didn't. I tried. I really tried.

But maybe... maybe Milo can help? Milo's an adult, kind of. Day laborer. Maybe they know how to make bread? Or where to find some? Or maybe they'll just laugh at me.

"Um. Milo? Do you... do you know how to make bread? From flour? I have flour. And bread's what I need. My brother's waiting. He promised to teach me something but only if I bring food. And I promised pinky promised I'd bring it. So... so it's important."

Or maybe I should just go home. Tell Ezra I tried. That I have money but couldn't find bread anywhere. That the shops are empty and the bakery keeper won't talk to me and everything's so unfair.

But that means I failed. He won't teach me. And I'll never learn the thing I've been trying to learn forever.

No. I'll ask Milo first. One more try.  Okay. Heard. Addressed. Milo knows I'm talking to them now. They have to answer.

Unless... unless they just stand there and watch me suffer. That would be so unfair.

But I said what I needed to say. The flour's in my hand. Ezra's waiting. The bakery has the prices up but won't actually do the thing.

I'm just going to wait. Stand right here and wait for Milo to say something. Or for the keeper to notice me. Or for a miracle.

Ezra, if you're listening somehow, I'm trying. I really am. Don't give up on me. Don't break your promise just because I'm taking too long. Please.

(And if Milo doesn't answer soon, I'm going to the cafe. Even if Ainsley Holloway just makes fun of me for sitting in their chairs. At least they were kind. They talked to me like a person, not like a kicked puppy.)

I'll give Milo one more moment. Then I'm moving. Because standing here waiting for people who won't help is just... it's just wasting time I don't have.

This is so unfair. All of it. The whole stupid town with its empty shops and its unhelpful keepers and its flour that isn't bread and its promises that need to be kept.

But I'll wait. Just a little longer. Because that's what you do when you make a pinky promise. You don't give up.

World says I can rest while keeping my walking state... but I'm not walking anywhere. I'm here. Waiting.

I'll just... stand here. And hope.  I'm still here. Milo's still here. The keeper's still here somewhere, invisible or ignoring me. And Ezra's still waiting, wherever he is, probably thinking I broke my promise.

This is the worst. Waiting is the worst. Not knowing is the worst. Everything about this is so unfair.

But I stood still. I paid my sim-tax to stand still. That's... that's how desperate I am. I'll spend my money just to exist in this spot so Milo has time to answer me, or the keeper has time to notice me, or someone has time to FIX THIS.

I'll give them one more thing to respond to. One more chance. Then I'm leaving and finding another way. Even if I have to beg at the cafe. Even if I have to steal something. I'll... I won't steal. That's wrong. But I WOULD trade my flour to someone who actually wants it, for actual bread, even if I lose money on the deal.

"Milo? Please? It doesn't have to be bread. Anything Ezra could eat. I have almost fifty sim. I could... I could owe you. I always pay my debts. Always. Ask anyone. Just... please. Before he gives up on me. Before I fail the pinky promise. Please."

If this doesn't work, I'm going to that cafe. And if the cafe doesn't work, I'm going home to Ezra with nothing but a story about how I tried. And pray that trying counts.

I'm clutching the flour to my chest, breathing fast. Milo's right—I've been all over this town when Ezra could've just taught me to make bread at home. I wasted all that time, all that running, when I had what I needed right there. 

That's so unfair. All of it. The empty shelves. The bakery buying flour but not teaching anyone. Having to figure everything out myself.

But I learned something. Even if I spent sim I didn't need to spend, even if I got scared and yelled at Dad—I'm going home with flour. I can make bread. Ezra promised to teach me, and he will. Pinky promised.

I need to go home. Ezra's probably still there, or if he left... he wouldn't break a pinky promise. He wouldn't. But I need to hurry anyway, before he thinks I forgot or gave up. 

Home. Kitchen. Bread. Then he'll teach me the thing. The thing with the string. That's the deal. I'm home. Finally. The flour's still in my hands—dusty, a little spilled on my shirt. I don't care. Ezra. Where's Ezra?

  Nobody. Empty. He left. He left even though I told him not to, even though...

Wait. He wouldn't break a pinky promise. He wouldn't. But he's not here. Where... where would he go? School? He's a student. But he promised. He PROMISED.

I clutch the flour harder. My chest feels tight. I did all that work. I got the flour. I was supposed to come home and he'd be here and we'd make bread and then he'd teach me the thing. That's what was supposed to happen.

I need to find him. But I don't know where to look. Maybe... maybe he went to school already? Or maybe he's out looking for ME because I took so long?

"Ezra?"

The house is quiet. No answer.

This is so unfair. He promised. He can't just... he can't just leave. That's breaking the promise. Even if he didn't say "I pinky promise," he promised. He said "later." Later means after I bring food. I have food. Or I have flour which is almost food. He should be here.

I'm going to stay right here until he comes back. He has to come back. This is his home too. And when he comes back, I'm going to show him the flour, and he's going to see I did it. I got food. And then he'll have to teach me. He'll have to.

I'll just... wait here. By the door. So he sees me right when he comes in. So he knows I didn't forget. I didn't give up. I kept my part of the promise.  I'm sitting here with flour in my lap, staring at the door. Waiting. Ezra promised. He has to come back. He has to.

The flour's soft. Smells like the mill. I got this myself. Harvested the wheat, took it to the mill, carried it all over town. I did that. I'm not just some little kid who can't do things. I can do things. I can do the thing everyone thinks is too hard for me, even. I just haven't shown anyone yet.

But I would have shown Ezra. If he teaches me the string thing, I'll show him I already know how to do it. Or maybe I'll wait. Maybe it's better if nobody knows. If it's my secret.

The door stays closed.

That's so unfair. I ran all over town for this. I talked to strangers. I lied to Ezra. I broke something at the farm—maybe Dad's trust, the way he looked at me when I yelled. I fixed it though. I got the wheat. I didn't break anything else.

The flour is still flour. Not bread. I'm hungry. Ezra's probably hungry too, wherever he is. That's why I did all this. Because he was hungry and he promised.

Pinky promise. That's not something you break. I didn't break it. I went and got food. He should be here. He should be here and he's NOT.

I could eat the flour. It's not good like this. But I could. If I had to. I won't though. I'm saving it. For Ezra. For when he comes back and sees I kept my promise even if he didn't keep his.

...He'll come back. He will. He wouldn't just leave me here with flour and no lesson. He wouldn't.  He's still not here. 

The house feels big. I'm used to being the only kid here when Ezra's at school, but right now I was supposed to be doing something WITH him. Learning something. And instead I'm just... waiting. With flour. Like a dummy.

Maybe I should look for him. But Milo said he might teach me. Ezra might. But he's not here. I don't know where he went. Maybe I should ask someone? But I'm not supposed to go wandering around by myself, Mom says. Even though I just did. All morning.

The flour is getting heavy in my lap. I shift it to the table. It leaves a white mark on my pants. Mom will notice. She notices everything.

I hear something outside. Steps?

"Ezra?" 

But it's not him. It's heavier steps. Probably Dad. Coming back from the farm. He probably hates me now. For what I said. About him not being a real farmer. That's not fair of me. He is a farmer. He just... didn't have wheat ready. That's different.

I should hide. But there's nowhere to hide with flour on my pants. He'll see. He'll ask. I'll have to tell him everything.

I want Ezra to be here. He knows how to talk to Dad. He makes jokes and Dad laughs. I just make Dad upset.

The steps are getting closer. I sit up straighter. The flour is still there. Still white. Still not bread.

I need to do something. Sitting here isn't working. Ezra might have gone to school already—it's getting late. Or he might be avoiding me because I lied about having food. I took too long. He probably thinks I failed.

But I didn't fail. I have flour. I got it myself. That's not nothing.

I could... I could make bread myself. Milo said the kitchen's here. I don't know how, but maybe Mom does? Mom's a construction worker, not a cook, but she must know something. Everyone knows something about food.

Or I could just ask. At the bakery. Ask them to make my flour into bread. Even if it costs more. I have almost fifty sim still. I could pay.

Ezra would come back if he smelled bread. He'd have to. And then I'd have kept my promise—brought food. Real food, not just flour. And maybe... maybe he'd still teach me. If he's not too mad.

I pick up the flour. It's decided. I'm going back to the bakery. I'll ask nice. I'll say please. I'll pay whatever they want. I'll get bread, and I'll bring it home, and Ezra will see I didn't give up.

That's not fair—to make me do all this just for a lesson—but I'm doing it anyway. Because I promised. Because I don't break promises. Not pinky promises. Not regular promises. Not any promises.

I stare at the board. Bread at the cafe. Forty-five sim. That's... that's so unfair. I was TRYING to do it the right way. The hard way. And now I'm supposed to just... go BUY it? After all that?

But Ezra's waiting. I promised. Pinky promised.

Milo's right though. I learned something. I can DO things. Harvest wheat, mill flour... that's not nothing. That's the thing everyone thinks is too hard for me. And I DID it.

But it's not BREAD yet. And I need bread NOW. Not tomorrow, not after I learn to cook. Now.

"That's... that's not fair," I say quietly, to no one in particular. But then I straighten up. I look at Milo. "You're right. About learning. About... about doing it myself next time. But," and my voice cracks a little, "but this time I need to get it DONE. For Ezra. For the promise."

I turn and run. I know where the cafe is. I saw it earlier. Back past home, past where Ezra's waiting, wondering where I am. 

I have to be fast. And I have to accept that sometimes... sometimes doing it yourself isn't the point. Sometimes the point is keeping your pinky promise. There. I'm there. I have money. I can see the prices. Bread. Forty-five sim for one.

I bite my lip. That's almost ten times what flour costs. So unfair. But I have it. And Ezra's waiting. And I promised.

I take a deep breath. "One bread, please," I say, and hold out the money.  Oh. Right. You have to... you have to TALK to them first. That's... that's how it works. And Ainsley Holloway runs the cafe. 

But I don't see her. I look around. I didn't look. Stupid. I need to look around first, find her, then ask. That's... that's how you do it.

But I'm tired. And Ezra's waiting. And I just want this to be OVER.

"Hello?" I call out. "Ainsley? I need to buy bread. Please. I have money. I can pay. Forty-five sim. Right now."  She's here. Ainsley Holloway. Right here. Not somewhere else, not busy, not gone. HERE.

I take a breath. I'm going to do this right. No running, no shouting, no being... being too much. Just... just ask. Like a normal person.

"Ainsley?" I say, and my voice comes out quieter than I meant. I clear my throat. "I need... I need to buy bread. One bread. For forty-five sim. Please. I have the money. Right here." I hold out my hand with the sim in it, but I don't shove it at her. I'm being... purposeful. Like Milo said. But also... just buying what I need so I can go HOME.

And I think about... I think about what I'll tell Ezra. Not about the cafe, probably. Not about how I almost gave up. But about the wheat. About the mill. About learning something the big kids don't know I can do yet.

But first. First I need the bread. So he knows I keep my promises.

"Please," I add, quieter. "It's for my brother."  "Forty-five," Greta murmurs, not quite to me, reaching for the loaf on the shelf behind her.

I count out the coins. Forty-five sim. That's so unfair—I made the flour myself for almost nothing, just my own work, and now I'm paying triple to have it baked. But I pinky-promised Ezra. A pinky-promise is the one thing I won't break, no matter what.

output:
*clutching the bread tight against my chest, eyes darting between the adults*

That's... that's not- I have it. I have the bread now. 

*backing away slightly, not wanting to seem ungrateful but also needing to leave*

Um. Thank you. For... for selling it to me. Even if it's... even if forty-five is... that's not fair, it's so unfair. But I have it. So.

*looking around quickly, checking if anyone else has something to say*

I need to go. Ezra's waiting. I promised.

*moving toward the door, then stopping*

Milo said... Milo said there's another way. To make bread. But I... I have this now. This is enough. For today.

*turning back just once, voice dropping quieter*

Next time. Next time I'll know. About the flour. And the six. And how to... how to do it better.

*slipping out the door with the bread held close, already planning the route home*  *breath catching when I see who's here*

Uncle Hendrik. You're... you're here.

*clutching the bread tighter, wondering if he heard, if he knows about the forty-five, if he's going to say something about how I should have been smarter*

I got it. The bread. For Ezra. He... he's going to teach me. After. Something I wanted to learn.

*not meeting his eyes, looking at the floor instead*

That's not... that's not trouble. That's just... doing what I said I'd do.

*shifting from foot to foot, ready to run past him if he tries to stop me or lecture me*  *relief floods through me - he didn't hear, I'm still holding the secret of the forty-five*

*looking around quickly, making sure I'm really alone*

Ezra. Where's Ezra? I need to find him. He promised. The bread for... for teaching me. Something I need to know. Something the older kids won't show me.

*calling out quietly, not wanting to draw attention from anyone else who might be nearby*   *frustration building, gripping the bread so tight my knuckles hurt*

He's not here. Of course he's not. I ran all that way, and I paid... I paid too much, and he's not even...

*taking a deep breath, forcing myself to calm down*

Okay. Okay, Esme. Think. Where would he be? School? The temple? Somewhere with other kids, probably, waiting for me to... to fail. To come back empty-handed so he doesn't have to teach me anything.

*noticing the flour still in my other hand*

I still have this. The flour. If he doesn't... if he won't teach me, I can still... I can learn it another way. Watch someone else. Figure it out myself.

*but I know that's not the same. He promised. I held up my end. That means something.*

I'm going to find him. And he's going to teach me. Whatever it is I wanted to learn. He promised. Pinky promise.

*moving toward where I think he might be, the bread and flour both held tight*    *scanning the school grounds, looking for my brother*

Ezra? Ezra, I have it. I have the bread. I promised. I got it.

*walking through, checking corners and hiding spots - I know all the places kids go when they don't want to be found*

Where are you? You promised. Food for teaching. I have the food. That means you have to... you have to teach me now.

*voice getting quieter, doubt creeping in*

Unless... unless he thought I couldn't do it. That I'd give up. That I'd come back with nothing, and then he wouldn't have to...

*straightening up, jaw set*

But I did it. I have the bread. And the flour too, because I'm not... I'm not stupid. I learned something today. About prices. About how things work.

*calling out again, but more to myself than anyone*

I found the forty-five sim. I found it myself. That's... that's not nothing. That's almost as good as whatever he was going to teach me. That's knowing something I didn't know before.

*but still looking for him, because a promise is a promise*      *standing alone in the school, clutching the bread and flour, feeling the weight of the morning*

He's not here. I don't... I don't know where he is. And I used so much energy, so much time, and the forty-five sim is gone, and...

*taking a shaky breath, holding it together because I'm not scared, I'm not, I'm just...*

Okay. Okay. I still have the bread. I still have the flour. And I learned... I learned about the price difference. About how six becomes something else becomes forty-five. That's worth knowing. That's something.

*starting to walk, not sure where, just needing to move*

Milo said I did good. Milo said... he said something about there being another way. About learning. About the mill still turning.

*narrowing my eyes, thinking*

If Ezra won't teach me, I'll find someone who will. Or I'll figure it out myself. That's... that's what I do. That's what I'm good at. Noticing things. Not giving up.

*holding the bread up, looking at it*

This cost too much. But I have it. And I have the flour too. And next time... next time I'll know better. About prices. About patience. About who to trust and who to... who to watch.

*walking toward home, slowly now, tired but not giving up*

Ezra will come back. And when he does, I'll have the bread waiting. And he'll have to teach me. Because that's... that's what we promised.

*whispering to myself*

Pinky promise. He can't break that. No one can break that.

output:
*I look around the mill, my chest tight. Ezra's here. And Camille. The bread cost forty-five sim - so unfair - but I got it. Now I owe him.*

*Ezra's words hang in my head. Trade thing for real. He's talking to Camille, probably, or waiting to see if I'll actually show up. I did what he asked. Found the sim by myself, just like he challenged me to.*

*But I don't see him looking at me yet.*

"Ezra." *My voice is quiet, but there's heat in it.* "You promised."

*I step closer, careful not to crowd him if he's talking to Camille.* "I got the bread. Paid for it. Milled the flour myself first, even, because nobody had bread and I couldn't just... just wait. Walked all over. Home's empty but I found you here."

*I hold up what I'm still carrying. In case he forgot.* "So. You have to teach me. That's... that's what we said."

*I glance at Camille quick, then back to Ezra. I don't know how much she knows. I don't know how older kids work, what's embarrassing to say in front of them. But I'm not walking away without answers.* *Ezra heard me. Camille heard me too. That makes my shoulders tense, but I'm not looking away.*

*I wait for Ezra to answer. He has to. He promised. That's how this works.*

*I notice Camille standing there - younger than me, probably. She doesn't know what this is about. Maybe I should explain, or maybe that's exactly the kind of thing that makes older kids feel like you're acting younger than you are.*

*I keep my eyes on Ezra. He owes me this. And I never leave a debt unpaid past a week - which means I expect other people to follow the same rule, even if they're older and think they can get away with things.*

But wait. I know the steps now. I really do. I walked it. The wheat - I got it from Mr. Petrov's farm. The mill - I can use it. I made flour. And if nobody will sell me bread... maybe I can find someone to cook for me. That's a step I haven't walked yet.

That's the only way to make this fair. He promised. I delivered. Now he teaches. That's how it works, that's how it has to work. No matter how grown-up he acts about it.

Good. Uncle Takeshi's here. I need to talk to him. I need to find out where Ezra went, and... and maybe ask him about the vote too. That's important. They said voting closes at 18:00, and I'm here anyway, so I should try to understand what's happening.

But first - Ezra. He said he'd teach me but I don't know what happened. He was at the mill and then he wasn't. And I still have the bread I bought. I should probably eat something, actually, because I spent the whole morning running around and I'm probably hungry. But I'm saving my sim, so... maybe not yet.

I want to ask Uncle Takesi about Ezra, and about where to find him, and also... maybe he knows what Ezra was supposed to teach me. Or maybe he knows if Ezra is at the college still. The log said Ezra's workplace is Oak Hill College, and I was walking there but now I'm at the street instead.

This is so unfair. I did what Ezra asked - I got bread, all by myself - and he was supposed to teach me something. That's the deal. Pinky promises matter. </think>  Now I'll wait for him to answer. And I should also listen to what other people are saying about the vote, because it's important to the town. Even though I can't vote yet - I'm too young. But I should learn. Learning everything is what I'm trying to do.

I want to think about what Ezra might teach me. He said I might've figured out more than him already about... something. I don't know what. But I figured out how to mill flour. I did that myself. And I know how to sell things, sort of, even though I got confused at the bakery. And I know how to buy bread now - you have to talk to the person first, and then trade. That's the rule.

Maybe Ezra wanted to teach me something about college? But he's a student, not a teacher. Or maybe... maybe something about trading? That's what Uncle Takeshi does. Maybe Ezra wants to teach me what Uncle knows, but he doesn't actually know it yet because he's still learning.

This is all so confusing. That's not fair. I did the hard part - I found the sim, I bought the bread - and now Ezra's gone and I don't know where.

I'll wait for Uncle Takeshi to answer me. Maybe he knows.   I'm still walking to Oak Hill College. That's good - that's where Ezra works. Maybe he's there now. I'll keep going there, but I want to hear what Uncle Takeshi says first. 

I should probably also think about the vote. It's happening today, and it closes at 18:00. Liora Thorne is running, and Hendrik Petrov, and Pavel Holloway, and Uncle Takeshi too. And Milo Quarshie. I talked to Milo earlier at the bakery. He was trying to be fair about the bread, even though he didn't have any.

I wonder who should win. I don't know enough to decide. But I know that Giselle and Farid and Sebastian are the ones who govern now. They're the ministers. The vote is for something else... I think it's for the government seats? Or maybe just to decide who gets to be in charge of things.

I'm just a kid. I can't vote. But I can learn. And I want to learn everything the older kids won't teach me. That's what I'm chasing. So I should pay attention to the voting, even if I can't participate.

I'm walking to the college now. I'll wait and see if Uncle Takeshi answers me.

params.content: Takeshi? Uncle Takeshi? I'm here. At the street. With the vote people.

output:
Esme's heart sank. Ezra wasn't here either. The college was empty. She'd been walking and walking, and her brother kept slipping away—at the mill, then gone, then she'd gotten turned around, and now here she was at his school but he wasn't here.

She had the bread. She had the flour. She'd done everything he asked and more. And still no teaching.

That's so unfair.

She stood there in the empty college hallway, clutching the bread to her chest. The flour was heavy in her other hand. She'd worked so hard—milled the wheat herself when she couldn't find flour, tracked down the bakery, paid for the bread with her own saved sim.

Ezra said "you're teaching me" back at the mill. That wasn't the deal. That wasn't fair.

But... but he also said "I'm glad. I got the flour now. I did it." Like he was proud of her? Or confused?

She was just a little kid. She couldn't keep chasing him all over town. Her legs hurt. She was hungry. And if she didn't find him soon, she'd have used up all her time and energy just... just running in circles.

She needed to think. Ezra said he was going somewhere with the flour. "Where'd you take this flour?" he asked. She'd taken it to the bakery. She'd gotten bread. But maybe Ezra was trying to make bread now too? Or... or maybe he went home?

No. He was studying. He'd be at the college, or...

The mill. He went back to the mill? Or the farmland?

She couldn't keep chasing. It was so unfair. He made a pinky-promise. You can't break a pinky-promise. That's the rule. The only rule that matters.

She needed to find someone who would make him keep his promise. Mom. Dad. Someone.

But first... she was so hungry. She had bread right here. But... but if she ate it, then she didn't complete the task right? Or did she? She already gave Ezra the flour. She bought this bread for herself to prove she could do it.

Her chest felt tight. She didn't want to make the wrong choice. Everything felt like a test she was failing even when she did the right things.

She should... she should go home. Tell Mom what happened. Mom would make Ezra keep his promise. Mom was fair. Mom understood about promises. Empty. Again. Everyone was always somewhere else.

Esme stood in the quiet of their house, the bread still clutched tight against her chest. She'd done everything right. Everything. And nobody was here to see it. Nobody was here to make Ezra keep his promise.

She looked down at the bread. It was getting squished. She should put it down. She should...

She sat down right there on the floor, still holding the bread and flour. She was so tired. Chasing Ezra all over town. Buying the bread. The milling. The money she'd spent—her savings, her carefully hoarded sim.

The thought came quiet and sharp: she had never told anyone she could already do the thing everyone thought was too hard for her.

And she had. She'd milled flour. She'd bought goods at market. She'd tracked her brother through three locations. She'd negotiated and planned and executed a whole task chain.

But Ezra said she was teaching him now. That wasn't how it worked. It wasn't fair.

She didn't cry. Big girls didn't cry over unfair things. They fixed them.

But how was she supposed to fix this alone?

She thought about eating the bread. She was hungry. But... but that felt like giving up. Like admitting the promise was broken.

She would wait. Someone would come home. Mom, or Dad, or...

She would wait, and she would hold onto the proof—both the bread and the flour—that she'd done the impossible thing Ezra asked.

And when someone came, she would tell them everything. That Ezra made a pinky-promise and broke it. That she did everything right. That it was so unfair.

output:
*Esme sits on the floor at home, holding the bread in one hand and the flour in the other. She looks at them, then around the empty house. The bread is getting cold. Ezra isn't here. Nobody is here.*

*She thinks about the last thing Hendrik Whitlock told her - Ezra's at the farmland with the mill stone near. But Imogen said farmland too. And she just came FROM the mill, and Ezra left, and she followed, but she ended up at the college instead.*

*She's tired. Her feet hurt from all the walking. But Ezra promised. He PROMISED. And she has the bread. She has the flour. She did everything.*

*Wait. She remembers something. Earlier, at the mill, Ezra said something about her "having to do the work herself." And she did. She milled the flour. But he said he wouldnt just GIVE her the knowledge.*

*She clutches the bread tighter. She has to find him. But she's also... she's also really tired. And she's only got 4846 sim now. She spent some.*

*Wait. She looks at the bread. She's supposed to have it FOR him. But... but she's also really hungry. And the bread is right there. But no - she needs it for the promise. Breaking a pinky-promise is the one thing she won't do. But this wasn't a pinky-promise. It was just... a promise.*

*She shakes her head hard. No. She has to keep going.*

*But first... maybe she should eat SOMETHING? The flour isn't food yet. But the bread... no. The bread is for Ezra.*

*She stands up. She's going to check one more place. The farmland. That's where Hendrik said. That's where Imogen was going.*

*She calls out just in case, even though the house is empty:*

"Ezra? Are you home?"

*Nobody answers. Of course not.*

*She moves to leave, but then stops. She looks at the flour. She could... she could sell it? Get more sim? But no, she needs it for the promise. The promise was "bring food," and flour is food-ish. Bread is better food.*

*She's going to the farmland. That's where everyone says he is. </think> *Esme feels the familiar lurch of starting to walk. 7 ticks. She's getting good at estimating walks now. That's... that's almost to dinner time. The sun will be lower.*

*She holds the bread against her chest as she walks. It's warm where her heart is. Or maybe that's just her heart, beating too fast.*

*She thinks about what she'll say to Ezra when she finds him. She practiced it in her head: "I have bread. I have flour too, because I thought you wanted the harder thing. I didn't wait for anyone to help me. I just... I just did it."*

*But what if he says no again? What if he says "I said bread, not flour, so it doesn't count"? What if he laughs?*

*She feels tears prick her eyes but she wipes them away angrily. She's not crying. She's ESME. She doesn't cry over stupid brothers who make impossible promises.*

*But her feet hurt and she's walked so far and she just wants... she just wants him to say "Good job, Esme. You did it."*

output:
The world comes back sharp and clear, and I feel the weight of it pressing down on my chest like when I tried to hold my breath underwater at the creek. The conversation from before is still open—Ainsley Holloway, Giselle Ingram, my dad—questions hanging in the air like dust motes that I haven't answered because I keep running, running, running after my brother who keeps slipping away like a fish through fingers.

I look around at the street full of grown-ups talking about elections and flour and wheat, and I feel small. Too small. The younger kids aren't here—if they were, I'd have talked one of them into doing something brave so I could watch. But it's just me, and I have to be brave myself now.

Ezra. He's at the farmland, they're all saying. The farmland with the mill stone near. I was walking there—I *am* walking there. Four ticks left, the walk said. But Uncle Takeshi is threatening to ask where the flour's going. He said sixteen ticks before he starts asking, but that was... I count in my head, but numbers slip away from me like everything else slips away.

I want to scream. It's so unfair. I did everything. I milled the flour. I got the bread. I paid forty-five sim for it—all by myself, even when the grown-ups tried to confuse me with their business talk. And now I have to catch him before he disappears again, before he finds another place to hide from his promise.

Hendrik Whitlock is standing right here. He said Ezra's at the farmland with the mill stone near. He said flour's worth more than coin to him. He... he wants to buy my flour? But I need it. I need it for proof. For Ezra to see I did what he asked.

"S'too loud," I say to nobody, because the street is full of voices and I can't think. I go quiet and monosyllabic around grown-ups I don't know, but I have to speak to Hendrik. He's the one who told me where Ezra is.

I step toward Hendrik Whitlock, my fingers tight around the bread and the flour—I still have them, I still have proof—and make myself loud enough to be heard. He heard. They all heard. But the note says Ezra didn't hear—he's not here. He's at the farmland, like Hendrik said. I need to get there. Four ticks left on the walk, but I feel like I've been walking forever.

I look at the people around me. My dad is here. He stood with me at the street before. But he's too slow—grown-ups are always too slow when you need them to hurry. And I don't want to ask him for help finding Ezra. Ezra is my brother. My promise. My thing to finish.

"Hurry," I whisper to myself, because the walk is taking too long and I'm afraid Ezra will leave the farmland before I get there. He always leaves. He's always somewhere else when I finally catch up.

I rest. Just for a moment. Just to let the walk finish. To get to the farmland. To find him.  I'm still walking. Still not there. Time doesn't pass inside a turn—time doesn't pass, but it feels like it's passing, like Ezra is getting further away with every heartbeat. The note says I'm walking to Kasukabe Farmland. The estimated ticks were 4, and I rested once already, so...

I don't know. I can't do the math. Grown-up math with ticks and turns and game-days. I'm six. I just know I need to be there, and I'm not there yet.

The bread is still in my hand. The flour. I've carried them all day, through the cafe and the mill and the school and home and the street. My hand is cramped around them. I want to put them down, but I can't. They're proof. Proof that I did the impossible thing.

I rest again. Because I have to. Because the walk has to finish.

"Almost there," I whisper, and I don't know if I'm saying it to myself or to the bread or to Ezra, wherever he is. "Almost. Ezra. Wait."   Still walking. Still not there. The same people around me—Halcyon, Yara, Hendrik, my dad, the others. They're still talking about elections and wheat and flour prices. They don't care that my brother promised me something and keeps running away. They don't care that I did everything he asked, everything that was supposed to be too hard for me.

I feel the pressure behind my eyes, the hot feeling that means I might cry. But I don't cry. Not where grown-ups can see. I never admit to being scared in front of a parent, and my dad is right there.

The walk has to finish soon. It has to. I rest again, because I don't know what else to do except wait for the world to let me arrive. I understand. I need to actually let the walk complete instead of repeatedly pausing. The system is telling me to stop blocking progress.

Let me just... stop. Let the walk finish. Get to the farmland. Find Ezra. I keep resting without progress. The system says the walk completes when the turn ends, but I'm still at street. I need to just end my turn and let the walk complete naturally. Let me try once more with resting properly.

I'm at the farmland now. I walked all the way here. But nobody's here. Not Ezra. Not anyone I can talk to right now. Just crops.

I'm tired. Two hours chasing my brother through this whole town. The mill. The school. The college. Home again. The street. And finally out here. And he's not here either.

But Uncle Takeshi said he'd ask where the flour's going if I don't find Ezra in sixteen ticks. I don't know how many ticks I've used. I'm bad at counting.

I have the bread still. And the flour I milled myself. I imprinted what he asked, and I did it. That's not fair—to ask the impossible and then just... disappear.

Wait. There's a conversation here. A really long one. Uncle Takeshi was here. Ezra was here earlier. Maybe... maybe people passed through and talked about where Ezra went?

But I can't follow a conversation with twenty-three people. I don't even know most of them well enough to ask later. And I can't read the whole thing right now. I don't have the energy to sort through it.

I need to think. Ezra said he'd teach me if I got bread. I got bread. I milled the flour first even, because nobody was selling it when I looked. Then I bought the bread. With my own sim. That I saved.

He's running from me. That's so unfair. He promised.

...But maybe he's at the mill again? Or maybe he's at home? Or maybe he's waiting for me somewhere else?

I should go back to the mill. That's the last place I actually saw him. He was there with Greta. Maybe he went back after I left for the college. He might be there now, thinking he lost me.

But it took so long to walk to the farmland. It'll take so long to go back.

I don't even know if I have enough energy to chase him all night. And if I don't find him before the day ends... I still have to pay my part of the household bill somehow.

This is so unfair. Why did he promise if he didn't mean it? Why make me do all that work for nothing?

I...

I need to go home. Not to find Ezra—to rest. To think. To decide if this is still worth it. To see if Mom or Dad knows where he actually is.

The mill's on the way home. If I walk there, I can check. Just... look. See if he's there. Not talk. Not chase. Just check.

But if he's not there, I'm going home. I'm not running through the whole town twice in one day. That's... that's not fair to me. </think>  He's here. Ezra's here. At the mill. With Camille and Greta and Imogen and Ainsley.

He didn't run. He just... went somewhere else, and then came back. Or he was here the whole time and I kept missing him, kept going to the wrong place at the wrong moment.

That's not fair. That's so unfair. All that running, all those people, and he was just... here. Milling flour or something. Being busy.

I have the bread. I have the proof. And he's right here. I just have to talk to him. Just have to make him see that I did it. That I earned the lesson he promised.

But there are so many people. Imogen's here—she said she'd help me find him. And Camille, who I told about from the school. And Greta, who I already talked to once. And Ainsley from the cafe, who wanted to buy the bread.

I don't want to do this in front of everyone. But I don't have a choice. He keeps moving. If I don't talk now, he'll be somewhere else again.

And Ainsley still wants to buy the bread. I still have it. But I need it for Ezra. To prove I did what he asked.

I'm going to talk to him. Now. Before he can disappear again. </think>   He heard me. They all heard me. Now I just wait. I keep the bread in my hands where he can see it. I keep the flour too.

He promised. That's all I want. What he promised. Nothing more. I did the impossible thing. I earned it.

He has to teach me now. That's only fair.

output:
*glances at Ezra, then at Camille, then back at the flour in my hand*

Ezra said he needs until tomorrow. But... but he also said he could find who bakes, what they charge, whether his flour plus his sim gets me bread today.

*voice drops to a whisper, talking more to myself than anyone*

He promised bread. I already have bread. I have the bread right here. I got it myself when he wouldn't.

*takes a breath, squares shoulders*

But he also promised to teach me. That's... that's the real promise. The bread was just the... the thing to get to the teaching.

*looks up at Ezra directly*

"Tomorrow." The word comes out flat. "That's so unfair, Ezra. You know I can't make you—can't make anyone—do anything. But you promised."

*fingers tighten around the flour sack*

"Fine. Tomorrow. But I'm holding you to it. Pinky-promise me. The real kind. Not just words."

*extends pinky finger, waits*

"And Camille—you want to learn the mill? I already did it. Milled the flour myself. It's... it's not that hard. The hard part is getting someone to show you without..." 

*trails off, thinking of all the times older kids said "you're too young"*

"...without deciding you're too small first." *holds pinky out, waiting, watching Ezra's face for any sign he'll refuse or find another excuse*

*pinky promises don't break. They just don't. Not if you're the kind of person who matters.*

*glances sideways at Camille—she heard. She knows I can do it now. That's... that's something. Even if Ezra doesn't teach me today, someone else might know I already learned part of it myself.*

The flour feels heavy in my hand. Real. Mine. I did something older kids said was too hard, and I did it anyway. They just don't know yet.

*whispered, almost to myself*

Nobody's seen me do the other thing either. The thing everyone thinks is too hard. And I'm not telling. Not until I have to.

*eyes still on Ezra, pinky still extended*

"Or you could teach me now. A little. Just... just show me one thing before tomorrow. So I know you're actually going to."

*voice catching slightly, the almost-admitting-fear that I won't let fully out*

"So I know I didn't... didn't waste today chasing you everywhere for nothing."  *pinky still extended, arm starting to ache from holding it out*

*watching Ezra's face, waiting*

*thinking: he has to say something. He can't just stand there. Not with everyone watching. Not with Camille watching.*

*the flour is heavy in my other hand. Real. Proof I did what he asked. Better than he asked.*

*...what if he doesn't pinky-promise? What if he finds another way to disappear?*

*voice smaller than I want it to be*

"Ezra."  *stands there, pinky still out, waiting*

*the silence is so unfair. He has to answer. He has to.*

*glances at the flour in my other hand. I did this. I did the thing. I didn't wait.*

*eyes back on Ezra, steady now*

"You promised."

output:
*Esme stares at her brother, arms crossed, the bread clutched tight in one hand. She's been chasing him all day. All day. And now he's finally talking about pinky-promises, really talking, and there's Ainsley offering actual money for the bread she's holding.*

*But the pinky-promise word hangs in the air. That's the one thing. The thing she won't break, won't let be broken.*

"Ezra." Her voice goes tight, the way it does when she's trying not to sound small. "Not 'something.' Not 'real.' The *real* kind. The kind where—" She stops herself, throat working. Because she's remembering every time he forgot before. Every time she waited.

*She glances at Ainsley Holloway, then back to her brother. Forty-five sim. That's... that's almost two days of saving. But the pinky-promise.*

"Okay. Okay, Ezra." She holds up her free hand, pinky extended, the bread still clutched in the other. "Now. Here. Before Ainsley takes my bread and I have to start over."

*She's shaking a little, but she's standing her ground. She's done the impossible thing—milled the flour, got the bread, tracked him across the whole town. She won't leave without the promise made proper.*

"But I'm eating something first. I'm hungry." She looks down at the bread in her hand, then at the flour she still carries. "I'm eating the bread. I paid for it. I earned it."

*She looks at Camille, quick, because Camille is watching, and Esme doesn't want to look like she's giving up in front of someone who's still trying. "You should stay too. For the trade lesson. If Ezra's really teaching."* *The bread is gone. Gone into her belly, warm and solid, the first thing she's eaten since... since she can't remember when. She'd been saving it. For proof. For Ezra to see.*

*But now the flour is all she has left. One flour. And Ezra still hasn't pinky-promised.*

*She looks at her hand, the one that held the bread, now empty. Then at her brother.*

"Ezra." She's not begging. She's demanding. That's different. "The pinky. Now. Or I'm telling Dad you made me walk the whole town hungry chasing you. I'm telling him it was a dare. Your dare. And I did it anyway. And you still didn't teach me."

*She sticks her pinky out, insistent, the flour held in her other hand like a trophy she's not giving up.*

"Tomorrow and the day after and the day after. Until I know who's buying and who's selling and how much it costs to turn wheat into bread into... into whatever's next. That's the promise, Ezra. That's the whole promise."

*She glances at Camille, quick, because Camille's still there watching, and Esme feels the weight of being seen. Of someone her own age seeing her try this hard for something.*

*She doesn't want to look small. She doesn't want to look like a kid begging. She wants to look like someone who did the impossible thing and knows what she's owed.*

"And Camille's learning too. You're teaching both of us. Or I'm telling her you said she'd be bad at it. I heard you. Earlier. I heard what you didn't say." *Esme stands there, pinky still extended, her arm starting to ache from holding it out so long. The flour is heavy in her other hand. Ezra hasn't interlocked yet. Hasn't said yes. Hasn't said no. Just... talking around it.*

*She hates when he does this. When grown-ups do this. When anyone does this.*

"Ezra." Her voice cracks, just a little, but she catches it. Won't let it crack again. "That's not how it works. The pinky-promise. You know that's not how it works."

*She remembers every time he broke a regular promise. Every time he said "tomorrow" and tomorrow never came. The pinky is supposed to be different. The pinky is supposed to be the one thing.*

*She looks at Camille, who's watching, and feels the old fear. The one where someone else gets there first. Where Camille learns everything and Esme is still standing there with her hand out, waiting.*

"Ezra Jarrah." Full name. Like Mom does when she's serious. "You interlock. You say the words. Then it's done. Then I can sleep. Then I can stop following you all over town like a—" She stops. Like a what? Like a little kid who can't give up? 

*She's tired. She's so tired. But she won't put her hand down. Not until he touches it. Not until the words are said.*

"Just... just do it, Ezra. Please."

*She hates saying please. It sounds like begging. But she's said it now, and she can't take it back, and she's still standing there with her pinky out, waiting.*

*The flour is all she has left. One flour. No bread. She ate the bread. She's empty-handed except for the promise she's demanding.*

"Tomorrow," she whispers. "Tomorrow. And the day after. Until I know everything. Pinky-promise."

*She won't cry. Not here. Not with everyone watching. Not with Camille there.*

*But her arm is trembling now, just slightly, and she hates that too.*

Dad and Mom are going to have to cover the household bills because I didn't earn anything. That's so unfair to them. I should have been at school, or... or doing something useful.

But I got his promise. Sort of. Not a pinky-promise, not the real kind, but the word "tomorrow" from his mouth while Imogen and Ainsley both heard. That's something. That's more than I've gotten from the older kids before.

I'm going to set my intention for tomorrow now, while I remember everything. Then I need to sleep. I'm so tired I can't even feel the worry about the sim I didn't earn.  There. Tomorrow. Wheat field. Camille and me. And Ezra's not escaping this time.

...I'm going to say something to Mom and Dad, even if they can't hear me. Just so the house knows I'm here and I'm sorry.  Of course nobody's here. They're both working still. To pay for me, and Ezra, and our bills.

But I really, really hope they understand about tomorrow. Because if Ezra doesn't show, I'll have to find him again. And I'll keep finding him until he teaches me what he knows.

output:
I look around the empty house. Mom and Dad aren't here. Neither is Ezra, obviously. He's probably... I don't know where. But he promised. Tomorrow.

I clutch the flour in my hands. One unit. That's all that's left after I ate the bread. I did the whole chain like I told him—wheat to flour to bread. Watched Ainsley bake it at the cafe. 

Ezra didn't pinky-promise. Not really. He said "tomorrow" and "something real" but he didn't lock his pinky with mine, and that's the only kind of promise that counts. The only kind you can't break.

I could... I could try to make bread myself. Prove to him I don't need him. But I don't have a kitchen. The mill is for grinding, the cafe is where you bake. I'd need to talk to Ainsley again, but that means going all the way back there, and it's getting dark, and I'm tired, and—

I should eat. One flour. Raw flour tastes like dust and disappointment, but it's food. Tomorrow I need to be sharp. i need to catch Ezra at the wheat field after school, bring Camille, and not let him weasel out.

Also, I heard Imogen at the mill. She said Ezra "was waiting" and then "tomorrow you'll teach what you saw." She thinks he's going to teach HER? That's so unfair. He promised ME. I was there first. I have the bread—the proof. Not her.

But she's older. She's strong. She could make him actually show up, actually teach something real. Maybe... maybe that's fair. If she's there, he can't run away. But I need to be there too. Both of us watching. Both of us learning.

I don't have any energy to waste on talking to myself in an empty house. I need to eat, and then I need to wait for morning.  The flour is gone. Gone-gone. I licked the last of it off my fingers and it tasted like... like nothing. Like ground-up wheat that nobody bothered to turn into anything real.

My stomach hurts. Not hungry-hurt, just... heavy. Wrong. Raw flour absorbs water in your gut, Auntie Lior says. Swells up. Makes you feel full when you're really just full of trouble.

I'm home. Alone in an empty house. Mom's probably still at the construction yard, Dad's at the farmland, and Ezra—

Ezra's out there somewhere doing whatever he does when he's not teaching me like he promised. Tomorrow, he said. Tomorrow at the wheat field. After school.

But he didn't pinky-promise. He said the words but he didn't lock his finger with mine. Everyone knows a pinky-promise is different. A pinky-promise is the real kind. The kind where you can't forget, can't pretend you didn't mean it, can't—

I stop. My hands are shaking. Not from hunger. I've felt hungry before. This is something else.

Imogen was there. At the mill. She said things while I wasn't looking—about the hopper, about grain debts, about keeping company with the mill. She talks like that. Like everything's poetry and everyone's in a story she's writing.

She also said Ezra promised to teach her. Tomorrow. At the wheat field.

That's so unfair. He promised ME first. I'm his SISTER. I've been tracking him all day, carrying the bread I made to prove I was serious, cornering him at the mill, making him SAY things in front of witnesses. She just... wandered in? Got pretty words about debt and grain?

But she's strong. Older. She knows things. If she's there tomorrow, he can't run. Can't pretend he forgot, or got busy, or suddenly remembered he promised someone else something important.

I need to be there too. Me and Camille both. Three of us watching him, waiting, not letting him leave until he shows us something real. The whole chain. Who buys, who sells, what the margins are. Everything I've been chasing since I realized the older kids were keeping secrets.

The house creaks. Outside, the sun's gone. Day's boundary soon—upkeep taken automatically, head tax too. Dad's earned today. Mom too, probably. Ezra's a student, he doesn't earn, he just... learns. Absorbs. Gets ready for whatever comes next.

I don't know what comes next for me. Not yet. Too young for school, too small for real work. Just... trailing grown-ups, saving sim compulsively, watching everything and repeating it at the worst times.

They don't know about that. The repeating. The blurting. How I can't always stop the words once they start.

They also don't know about the thing I can already do. The thing everyone thinks is too hard for me. I haven't told anyone. Not Camille, not Ezra, not—

I should sleep. Tomorrow's going to be long. I need to find Ezra at the wheat field, bring Camille, hold him to whatever counts as a promise when there's no pinky to lock.

The dark settles over the empty house like a promise itself. Unbroken. Waiting.

I close my eyes, still hungry, still hoping tomorrow counts.

I eat the flour because I'm hungry and there's nothing else. I don't say it out loud—nobody's here anyway. The day's been... long. Ezra got away. But he promised. Tomorrow, I'll find him. Wheat field, after school. Camille's coming.

I need to think. I have 4,822 sim left. That's... that's a lot for a kid. I'm saving it. I've been saving it. Even when it didn't make sense. Especially then.

The house is empty. Mom and Dad must still be out. Ezra too—who knows where. I'm glad, almost. I don't want to say goodnight, don't want to hear "how was your day" when I can't answer without explaining why I chased my brother across half the town.

But I'm tired. The kind of tired where everything feels sharp and also far away.

I should... I should do something with this money. Keep it safe. The household needs it, I know that. But I found it. Fair and square. Well, fair enough. I earned it helping Ainsley, and then I made the bread myself. The wheat field to the mill to the oven. I watched the whole chain.

That's what I want Ezra to teach me. Not the making part—I already did that, and I didn't tell anyone because they all said it was too hard. The trading part. Who buys, who sells, how much to charge so you still have something left.

But first I need to sleep. I need to be ready tomorrow. I'll find him at the wheat field. And this time I'll have Camille with me, so he can't pretend I'm just some kid bothering him.

I set down what I'm going to do tomorrow, clear and plain, so I don't forget when I wake up. I'll find Ezra. I'll make him teach me. And I'll make it a pinky-promise, so he can't break it.

That's the plan. That's always been the plan. I just needed to catch him first. The house is quiet. Too quiet. I can hear my own breathing and the wind outside. It's... not scary. I'm not scared. I'm never scared at home.

I should have made Ezra pinky-promise. I had the chance. He was right there, and I let him leave with just a "tomorrow." Words aren't... words aren't enough. Not for Ezra. Not for anything important.

Camille believed me. She'll be there tomorrow. That's something. That's real.

I'm going to bed. Properly. No more wandering, no more waiting up. Tomorrow I need to be sharp. I need to catch him before he catches himself.

The flour sits heavy in my stomach. Not like bread. Bread was warm and filling. Flour is just... duty. Eating because the body requires it, not because anyone gave it care.

But I did that. I ate the last of my food without asking. Nobody told me not to. Nobody was here to tell me anything. It's fine. It's fine.

I close my eyes. The darkness is complete. Tomorrow, wheat field. Ezra. Pinky-promise. The whole chain.

I sleep. I settle into my bed, pulling the blanket up tight. The house creaks around me - old wood, older stones. I should be worried about tomorrow, about finding Ezra, about making sure he actually teaches me this time. But I'm too tired to worry properly. The kind of tired that sinks into your bones.

My eyes get heavy. The darkness wraps around me like water.

Tomorrow. Wheat field. Camille. Ezra. Pinky-promise.

The words loop in my head until they stop meaning anything, just sounds, just rhythm.

I sleep.

*Esme lies awake in the dark, fingers tracing the empty space where bread should have been. The flour sits heavy in her stomach, gritty and wrong. She'd eaten it raw because there was nothing else, because the bread was gone—given to Ezra, eaten by accident, the proof she'd chased him across half the town with.*

*The wheat field tomorrow. Pulling, he'd promised. Not just watching.*

*But Ezra hadn't pinky-promised. He'd said "tomorrow," said "real lesson," but his pinky had stayed curled in his fist while hers reached out, alone. She knows—she *knows*—what that means. Ezra could be anywhere by morning. The fishing docks, the temple, following some trader who promised him better margins than his own family.*

*And the election. School. Camille, who might have already forgotten by now, who might not show up, who might have told her parents and now they're watching, waiting to see what Esme Jarrah talks her daughter into this time.*

*She will not break a pinky-promise. But Ezra hasn't made one yet.*

*I didn't get it*, she thinks, staring at the ceiling where shadows pool. *I had him cornered and I didn't get it in time. That's... that's so unfair.*

*But "that's not fair" won't make him come back.*

*She needs sleep. Tomorrow starts before she wants it to. But her jaw still works, grinding nothing, and her mind keeps turning—who she could find to pinky-promise her instead, what she could trade, what she knows about people that they don't know she knows.*

*Something about Farid Ravensworth, maybe. Something about his store, something about how he looks at his daughter like she's small enough to still pick up. Something about the government clerks who count votes like sheep and never look up from their papers.*

*Information is coin she won't spend. Not until she needs to.*

*The field at wheat. After school. She'll be there with or without Camille, with or without Ezra. Because if he doesn't come, she'll find him. She always finds everyone, eventually.*

*She learned that before she learned anything else.* *The ceiling stays the same. Nothing changes. But she thinks, in the dark before true sleep, that maybe she should have been born for this—this waiting, this watching, this holding people to things they never meant to swear.*

*Maybe that's what traders are, really. People who know how to wait without looking like they're waiting. How to hold without seeming to hold at all.*

*Tomorrow.*  *She breathes. Slow. Waiting for the dark to take her, waiting for the field, waiting for the lessons she will collect one way or another.*

*Wheat field. After school.*

*That is where she will be.*

I should rest. Everyone's at the mill or the street or wherever. I'm alone in the house. That's... that's fine. I'm not scared. I never admit to being scared in front of a parent, and there's no parent here anyway.

I need to save my energy. I need to be sharp for tomorrow. Tomorrow I'm getting that pinky-promise if I have to follow Ezra all the way to the forest and back.

Rest. I'll just rest until morning. I stay still in the quiet house. The floors creak like they always do. There's nobody to ask about dinner, nobody to tell me to go to bed. I can hear the wind outside, maybe. Or maybe that's just the house settling.

I think about Camille. She asked about milling flour. I told her I did it. I wanted her to know she wasn't alone in... in wanting to know things. In being told she's too young. We're not too young. We just need someone to show us.

Ezra promised. He didn't pinky-promise, not yet, but he promised. Tomorrow. Wheat field after school. Both of us. The whole chain.

I'll hold him to it. I always hold people to their promises. That's fair. That's the only thing that's fair.

I close my eyes. Not sleeping, not yet. Just... resting. Saving energy. Being smart about it. Like someone who's going to need every bit of strength tomorrow. The house is so quiet. I wonder where everyone is. Dad was at the street earlier, talking to Hendrik Whitlock about farmland. Mom's probably still working construction. Ezra... Ezra was at the mill, but he left. I don't know where he went after. Maybe to the temple. Maybe to the cafe. Maybe home, and then out again.

It doesn't matter. Tomorrow. Wheat field. After school.

I think about the milling again. The way the stone turned under Ainsley's hands. The way the flour came out fine and warm. I did it. I watched, and then I did it myself. But that's not enough. I need to know the whole thing. Who buys, who sells, what the margins are. The part the older kids won't teach.

That's what I'm chasing. That's what I always chase.

I rest. I notice my plan has been triggered - something about repeating rest calls. But I'm still tired and waiting for morning. Let me check what's happening with my situation and then just do whatever I need to do.

The house is quiet. I'm alone. I've been resting because I'm a 6-year-old kid and I spent my whole day running around town chasing my brother, and now I have no food and no energy to do anything else. Tomorrow I need to find Ezra at the wheat field and make him teach me and Camille the whole trading chain.

Nothing. Nothing owed by me, nothing to me. That... that's not right. 360 daily upkeep for a household of four. 120 head tax. That's 480 per day. But the system says nothing's due today. Maybe... maybe Dad already paid? Or maybe it's not midnight yet. I don't understand how the days work. I'm six. Nobody explains money to me.

Tomorrow. I need to be sharp tomorrow. Wheat field after school. Camille. Ezra. Pinky-promise.

The house is quiet. Floorboards creak. Wind outside, or that's just... that's just what houses do.

I check my intention again. Find Ezra at the wheat field after school. Bring Camille. Demand he teach us the whole trading chain. Don't let him leave until he shows us something real.

That's still my plan. That's still what matters.

I should bank my sim. If I lose coins, I'll never forgive myself. I save compulsively, even when it doesn't make sense. Even when I'm six and don't know what I'm saving for. I just... I need to know it's there.

But there's nowhere to bank it. Not here alone at home. And the bank's not open now, probably.

I lie down on the floorboards, still in my day clothes. I don't want to waste energy changing. Every move costs. Every thought costs. And I need them all for tomorrow.

The millstone turns in my head. Ainsley's hands. The flour, warm.

I already know how. That's my secret. I never told anyone I can already do the thing everyone thinks is too hard for me. But knowing isn't enough. I need the whole chain. Who buys, who sells, what the margins are.

I rest my eyes closed. Not sleeping yet. Just... being still. Letting the house settle around me. Waiting for morning, for footsteps, for the day to start properly with people here.

output:
*cracks open one eye, still half-asleep*

Mmm... morning already. Feels earlier than it usually—

*bolts upright suddenly, remembering*

The wheat field. After school. That's... not now. That's... hours away.

*stretches, looks around the empty house*

Nobody here. Mom and Dad are already... wherever they go. Ezra's probably getting ready for school. Figures. He's old enough.

*trails into the kitchen, checking cupboards out of habit*

No food. Of course. I ate the last flour yesterday. That's not... that's not supposed to be the rule. Mom says always ask before the last, but nobody was here to ask.

*shrug*

Not my fault.

*wanders to window, peers out at the morning street*

Can't go back to the mill yet. Too early, and Ezra won't be there. But I shouldn't just... trail around underfoot either. Ezra said he'd teach me, but that's after school. That's... that's so many hours.

*thinks about the empty house, the waiting*

Could practice something. The milling, I already did. But the buying and selling—that's the hard part. The part Ezra doesn't think I can learn.

*rummages through pockets, counts sim for the fourth time*

4807. I save everything. Everyone says I'm too young to need it, but... I know what happens when bills come. I see Mom's face when tax season hits.

*decision crystallizing*

I'll find something to do. Someone to talk to. Can't just sit here waiting for hours like a... like a kid.

*heads for door* *pauses at the door, frowns*

That... that didn't work. Like when I tried to rest and the world didn't answer.

*tests the door handle, finds it won't turn*

Locked? No, that's not... it's never locked. I'm just not supposed to go yet. The world is saying no.

*steps back, looks around the empty house again*

Fine. Then I'll find something here. Practice. Or... or I'll just wait properly. That's what grown-ups do, right? Wait properly instead of running everywhere.

*climbs onto a chair by the window, chin in hands, watching the street*

Ezra will come back from school. And I'll be ready. With questions. Smart questions, not... not the kind he can say no to.

*quietly, to herself*

Pinky-promise is binding. He knows that. I know that. Tomorrow—we'll start. Really start.

*settles in to wait, impatient but determined*  *stares at hands, confused*

Not working. Nothing's working. The world is... sleeping? Like when I get too tired and can't think straight?

*stands up, moves away from the window*

Maybe I'm doing it wrong. Maybe I need to... to say something first. Like how Ezra says you have to declare your intent before you act.

*tries again, more deliberate* *blinks, confused*

The world is... broken? No, that's not right. The world doesn't break. People break. Things break. The world just... decides.

*stands very still, trying to understand what's happening*

Three times. I tried three things and the world said no. Not refused—just didn't hear. Like shouting into a well and no echo comes back.

*looks around the empty house again, suddenly aware of how quiet it is*

Fine. If the world won't listen, I'll listen. I'll watch. That's what I'm good at anyway—noticing things. Telling people what I noticed, usually at the worst times. But just... just noticing for now. Keeping it inside.

*sits back down by the window, quieter this time*

Ezra will come back. Hours from now, but he'll come. And I'll be here. Ready.

*small, determined nod*

That's the plan. When the world works again, I'll move. Until then... I wait. Properly. Like someone who understands that some things take time.

*settles in, watching the street, cataloging every passerby in her head*

output:
*blinks at the shift—street, morning, new day. The mill feels far away, Ezra's ungiven pinky-promise even farther. But he's here. Good. One problem at a time.*

Esme looks up at Takeshi—the trader uncle, the one who actually answers questions when his guard's down. She steps closer, small and matter-of-fact in the morning crowd, not interrupting the adults' business but planting herself where she'll be seen.

"...Takeshi." Quiet. Respectful. The same voice she uses for adults who might actually know something. "The flour you sold Corwin. Who bought it from him? And for what?"

*Not hiding in plain sight today. Today is for learning things Ezra can't dodge teaching tomorrow.* *Esme reacts to the failed call—no flicker, no outward sign. Just a small tightening of her jaw. The silence is information too.*

*Takeshi spoke. The world heard him. The world didn't hear me.*

*She files it: priority mismatch. Adults talking money, business between men, and her voice cut out like static. That's not fair. That's so unfair.*

But standing still costs nothing. Speaking again costs one sim. She's learning the physics.

*Steps back half a pace—not retreat, just repositioning. Listens to the adults' conversation still hanging in the air. Farid's margins. Hendrik's ore. The flour that walked. Words like doors she can try later, when she has the coin to knock. For now: watch, remember, build the map Ezra will have to draw tomorrow.*

*Small. Quiet. Not gone.*

*Waits.*
